Q: How to use optional chaining to shorten this C# code? A:
  1. is there optional chaining in C# like in javascript?

Yes.
Optional chaining in JavaScript is a concise syntax to deal with null or empty values:

The optional chaining (?.) operator accesses an object's property or calls a function. If the object accessed or function called using this operator is undefined or null, the expression short circuits and evaluates to undefined instead of throwing an error.

Something very similar exists in C# since version 6.0:
It is the Null-Conditional Operator.
So you can write (like in JavaScript) something like:

var val = a?.b?.c;

(where a and b might be null)

  1. How can we convert this into optional chaining to shorten the code?

Optional chaining was the appropriate tool if your logic was purely null-checking.
But since it is not (you check for parsing validity), I don't think optional chaining can really help.
Regarding improvement(s): I guess it is a matter of personal preference, but I don't see any problem with your approach.
The only thing that could be relevant is that if you need to parse a lot of values, you could use Parse instead of TryParse and handle all possible errors in one place (an exception handler in this case).

Q: How to swap keys and values in a hash A:

here is why `Hash#invert` is a poor implementation:

> h = {a: :one, b: :two, c: :three}

 => {a: :one, b: :two, c: :three}

> h.invert.invert == h # it only works for the simplest case

 => true

But it destroys data for hashes where the same value appears multiple times - which in practice can happen easily:


> h2 = {cats: 2, birds: 2, dogs: 1}

 => {cats: 2, birds: 2, dogs: 1}

> h2.invert.invert == h  # FAIL!

 => false 

> h2.invert

 => {2 => :birds, 1 => :dogs} # destroying information! FAIL!!

> h2.invert.invert

 => {birds: 2, dogs: 1} # mathematically INCORRECT

The mathematically correct way to "invert" a hash is:

# this doesn't looks quite as elegant as the other solutions here,  
# but if you call inverse twice, it will preserve the elements of the original hash  
  
# true inversion of Ruby Hash / preserves all elements in original hash  
# e.g. hash.inverse.inverse \~ h  
  
class Hash  
  
  def inverse  
    i = Hash.new  
    self.each_pair{ |k,v|  
      if (v.class == Array)  
        v.each{ |x|  
          i[x] = i.has_key?(x) ? [k,i[x]].flatten : k  
        }  
      else  
        i[v] = i.has_key?(v) ? [k,i[v]].flatten : k  
      end  
    }  
    return i  
  end  
  
end

Hash#inverse gives you:


> h2 = {cats: 2, birds: 2, dogs: 1}
 => {cats: 2, birds: 2, dogs: 1}
> h2.inverse.inverse == h2
 => true                         # true-ish because order might change

> h2.inverse
 => {2 => [:birds, :cats], 1 => :dogs}
> h2.inverse.inverse
 => {birds: 2, cats: 2, dogs: 1} # order might not be preserved

See also: Ruby Cookbook
